blocks.text: This was the use of the word crocodile among the most ancient Greeks. But the same Greeks, having transferred the name to the beasts of the Nile, gradually took it away from lizards. Except that they did not cease to call by this name certain foreign species of that kind which seemed remarkable above the rest in use, shape or size, or to come closer to the form of the larger crocodile. Yet the epithet land was generally added, to distinguish them from the river crocodile. Thus Aristotle, History, book 2, chapter 17, on the belly of animals, says that the belly is of the same structure τοῖς κροκοδείλοις ἀμφοῖν [tois krokodeilois amphoin], in both crocodiles, that is, the land as well as the aquatic. And in book 5, chapter 33: Τίκτουσι δὲ καὶ σαῦροι, καὶ κροκόδειλοι οἱ [II, 483] χερσαῖοι, καὶ οἱ ποταμιοὶ, εἰς τὴν γῆν [Tiktousi de kai sauroi, kai krokodeiloi hoi chersaioi, kai hoi potamioi, eis tēn gēn]. Apollonius, Marvels, chapter 39, from Aristotle's Extracts τῶν ἀνατομῶν [tōn anatomōn]: Ὄφις ὤφθη ἐν Πάφῳ πόδας ἔχων δύο, ὁμοίους χερσαίῳ κροκοδείλῳ [Ophis ōphthē en Paphō podas echōn dyo, homoious chersaiō krokodeilō]. Aelian, History, book 1, chapter 58: Καὶ αἱ σαῦραι δὲ ἐπιβουλεύουσι ταῖς μελίτταις, καὶ οἱ κροκόδειλοι οἱ χερσαῖοι [Kai hai saurai de epibouleuousi tais melittais, kai hoi krokodeiloi hoi chersaioi]. And in book 16, chapter 6, on the Indian phattages: Ἐν Ἰνδοῖς γίνεται ζῶον κροκοδείλῳ χερσαίῳ παραπλήσιον ἰδεῖν [En Indois ginetai zōon krokodeilō chersaiō paraplēsion idein], etc. The Scholiast on Nicander, on the salamander: Ἔοικε δὲ τῷ χερσαίῳ κροκοδείλῳ [Eoike de tō chersaiō krokodeilō]. Jerome, Against Jovinian, book 2, chapter 6: Although the Syrians used to eat land crocodiles too, and the Africans even green lizards. Accordingly Hesychius, to show that the name crocodile is a homonym applying to both, says: Κροκόδειλος, τὸ ζῶον· καὶ τὸ ἐν τῷ Νείλῳ, καὶ τὸ χερσαῖον [Krokodeilos, to zōon; kai to en tō Neilō, kai to chersaion]. Meanwhile it is not sufficiently established which species of lizards, exactly, are given the name land crocodile. In his Corinthiaca Pausanias writes as though there were no other lizards of this name than those large ones two cubits long in Mauretania in Libya. For these are his words: Λιβύη μέν γε μόνη κροκοδείλους τρέφει χερσαίους διπήχεων οὐκ ἐλάσσονας [Libyē men ge monē krokodeilous trephei chersaious dipēcheōn ouk elassonas]. In Herodotus the same are said to be κροκόδειλοι, ὅσον τε τριπήχεες χερσαῖοι, τῇσι σαυρῇσι ἐμφερέστατοι [krokodeiloi, hoson te tripēchees chersaioi, tēsi saurēsi empherestatoi], crocodiles about three cubits long, living on land, very like lizards. Strabo calls [col. 1061] them σαύρας, διπήχεις [sauras, dipēcheis]. And Aristotle describes similar ones in Arabia, if these words of Aelian, book 16, chapter 41, are true: Σαύρους δὲ Ἀριστοτέλης ἐν τῇ τῶν Ἀράβων γῇ τίκτεσθαί φησι, καὶ δύο πήχεις ἔχειν αὐτούς [Saurous de Aristotelēs en tē tōn Arabōn gē tiktesthai phēsi, kai dyo pēcheis echein autous]. But in the passage of Aristotle from which Aelian drew this, they are said only to be πηχυαῖοι [pēchyaioi], a cubit long, nowhere διπήχεις [dipēcheis], two cubits long. The words are in the History, book 8, chapter 28: Ἐν δὲ τῇ Ἀραβίᾳ σαῦροι μείζους πηχυαίων [En de tē Arabia sauroi meizous pēchyaiōn]. Hence Pliny, book 8, chapter 39: The lizards of Arabia are a cubit long. In Dioscorides the skink and the land crocodile differ only as species and genus. For he defines the skink as κροκόδειλον χερσαῖον ἰδιογενῆ [krokodeilon chersaion idiogenē], a land crocodile of its own kind. But Pliny rebukes those who hold this view and assigns to the skink definite marks by which it may be distinguished from the land crocodile, though how truly, I do not quite know: Of the same likeness, he says, is the skink, which some have said is a land crocodile, only with a whiter and thinner skin. Its chief difference from the crocodile, however, is recognized in that the set of its scales is turned toward the head. Some of the moderns use skink and land crocodile indiscriminately, as if they were the same animal. So Gesner, Rondeletius and Marcellus Vergilius on Dioscorides. Others imagine the land crocodile to be a huge beast, almost equal to the river crocodile. See Bellonius, and Cardano, book 9, On Subtlety.
